To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

transcranial magnetic brain stimulation of the frontal eye field during saccade triggering has a facilitatory effect when applied simultaneously with target presentation, and has an inhibitory effect when applied after target presentation, but has no effect when applied during target presentation.
the right frontal eye field can be used to facilitate and inhibit the triggering of s accades in the gap paradigm.

the triggering of a saccade is facilitated if the frontal eye field is stimulated simultaneously with onset of a lateral visual target and is inhibited if the stimulation is applied after the end of target presentation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of single‐pulse stimulation of the frontal eye field in a modified gap and overlap paradigm with flashed presentation.
the effect of single pulse transcranial magnetic simulation on the triggering of voluntary saccades.
the effects of a single‐pulse trans‐cranial magnetic stimulation of the right frontal eye field on saccade latency in modified gap and overlap paradigm.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
transcranial magnetic single‐pulse stimulation of the frontal eye field is able to influence saccade triggering in a time interval‐specific manner.
transcranial magnetic simulation can facilitate or inhibit saccades in a paradigm‐dependent manner.
the effect of single transcranial magnetic stimuli is dependent on the paradigm used and the time interval of stimulation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

transcranial magnetic single‐pulses can facilitate or inhibit saccade‐triggering, but that the direction of effect and the underlying mechanisms depend on the time interval of the stimulation and on the experimental paradigm.

single‐pulse transcrainial magnetic stimulation of the frontal eye field has a facilitatory effect on triggering of contralateral, but not of ipsilateral saccades, if it is applied simultaneously with target presentation.
single‐pulse transcrainal magnetic stimulation can influence saccade triggering in a time‐dependent and paradigm‐dependent manner.
The main takeaway from our work is that
transcranial magnetic simulation over the frontal eye fields has the potential to modulate saccadic behaviour.
the effects of transcranial magnetic brain stimulation on the triggering and execution of eye movements are highly dependent on the timing of stimulation and the experimental paradigm used.
the effect of single pulse transcranial magnetic stimulations on saccade initiation is dependent on the time interval between the stimulation and the target presentation.
